clinicalPearls: Dilatation and shortening of the major subareolar (lactiferous) ducts, usually affecting peri- and postmenopausal women.
Classic presentation is thick, cheesy, multicoloured nipple discharge (creamy, green or brown) from multiple ducts, often bilateral.
Slit-like or transverse nipple retraction may develop as periductal fibrosis shortens the ducts and can mimic malignant retraction.
A firm subareolar mass or thickening can form and, with associated calcification, may raise concern on mammography.
Distinct from periductal mastitis, which affects younger smokers, although the two overlap within the duct ectasia-periductal mastitis spectrum.
Coarse, rod-like ('needle-shaped') secretory calcifications aligned toward the nipple are a characteristic benign mammographic feature.
Most cases need only reassurance once malignancy is excluded; total duct excision is reserved for troublesome discharge or recurrent problems.
Blood-stained single-duct discharge should not be assumed to be duct ectasia and warrants investigation for papilloma or carcinoma.
reference.pathophysiology: Mammary duct ectasia is a benign involutional process in which the large subareolar ducts dilate and fill with inspissated proteinaceous and lipid-rich secretions. Stagnant secretions may leak into the periductal tissue, provoking a chronic inflammatory reaction rich in plasma cells and macrophages (giving the alternative term plasma cell mastitis) and progressive periductal fibrosis. This fibrosis shortens the ducts, producing nipple retraction, while the retained secretions calcify to form the characteristic coarse ductal calcifications. The condition sits at the involutional end of the duct ectasia-periductal mastitis spectrum and is more prevalent with advancing age.
additionalDifferentials: Ductal carcinoma in situ presenting with discharge or calcification
additionalInvestigations: Triple assessment with examination, ultrasound and mammography
Assessment of discharge for single- versus multiple-duct and colour
Mammography to characterise secretory calcification and exclude malignancy
Ultrasound of any subareolar mass or dilated duct
Core biopsy of a discrete or suspicious mass
Ductography or ductoscopy in selected discharge cases
Serum prolactin and thyroid function if galactorrhoea is suspected
redFlags: A hard, irregular or fixed subareolar mass
Fine pleomorphic or branching microcalcification rather than coarse secretory calcification
Eczematous or ulcerated nipple change suggesting Paget's disease
Progressive unilateral nipple retraction with skin distortion
reference.prognosis: Duct ectasia is a benign, self-limiting condition that does not increase breast cancer risk. Symptoms often settle spontaneously, and surgery, when required for persistent discharge or retraction, is generally curative.
pitfalls: Assuming all nipple retraction is malignant, or conversely dismissing malignant retraction as benign ectasia
Failing to distinguish benign coarse secretory calcification from suspicious pleomorphic microcalcification
Attributing blood-stained single-duct discharge to ectasia without excluding papilloma or carcinoma
Confusing duct ectasia with periductal mastitis and mismanaging the younger smoker
Overlooking hyperprolactinaemia when discharge is milky and bilateral
references: Standard textbook of breast surgery on benign duct disorders
National guidance on investigation of nipple discharge
management: Complete triple assessment to exclude malignancy, then reassure that this is a benign, self-limiting involutional condition that does not raise breast cancer risk
Manage conservatively with warm compresses, good nipple hygiene and a well-fitting supportive bra
Reserve antibiotics for superimposed periductal infection, covering anaerobes and skin flora
Advise smoking cessation given its association within the duct ectasia-periductal mastitis spectrum
Offer surgical duct excision (microdochectomy or total duct excision) for persistent troublesome discharge or nipple retraction
Re-biopsy or investigate any suspicious mass or bloody single-duct discharge to exclude underlying carcinoma
